flights.title: AGE IS NOT A FLAVOUR
flights.tag: 6 core + 4 extensions · ALL BLIND · THREE PAIRS. IN EACH PAIR, WHICH IS OLDER — AND WHICH DO YOU PREFER?
flights.premise: Three pairs, poured as pairs, all bourbon. One grain family, one wood convention, new charred oak throughout — so every difference the room tastes traces to age rather than to Kentucky against Scotland. In each pair the ask is the same two questions: which is older, and which do you like more. Asked alone, "which is older" is a colour test. Asked together, the two questions come apart, and that gap is the flight.
why: Gold = the finale. Rust = pour blind, no introduction. Grey = reference or bench pour. Colour, nose, palate and finish are prompts — say them after the room speaks, never before.

PAIR ONE, A AND B — TWO YEARS, AND $150. Same distillery, same mashbill, two years apart. Two years is the hardest gap in the flight: past where age is obvious, short of where it is inaudible. Then give them the second fact. The 10 lists at $42.99, the 12 at $49.99 — and the 12 cost $199 to actually buy. Ask whether two years is worth a hundred and fifty dollars, after they have tasted it and not before.

PAIR TWO, C AND D — THE CONTROL, LOCKED BY LAW. Both Heaven Hill, both bottled-in-bond, which legally fixes one distillery, one distilling season and 100 proof. Three years apart and nothing else differs — not proof, not producer, not standard. This is the cleanest age comparison money can buy, and it exists because a law from 1897 says so.

PAIR THREE, E AND F — SIXTEEN YEARS AGAINST NONE, AND THE YOUNGER IS STRONGER. Same brand, same high-rye Beam mashbill. One is sixteen years old at 100 proof and costs $199.99. The other carries no age statement, runs 114 proof, and costs $32.99. The room will call F bigger, because it is — and bigger is not older. That is the trap, and it replaces the colour trap the all-bourbon build gave up.

THE SECOND COLUMN IS THE POINT. Age is not a flavour — it is a set of trade-offs. More wood, less spirit, softer edges, and past a point, diminishing returns and drying tannin. Two of the three pairs put a price on it. When someone correctly picks the older whiskey and then says they prefer the younger, the flight has done its job. Its companion, No Age Stated, asks the same question of whiskies that never printed a number.
Do not tell them it is three pairs until after the reveal. Pour A through F straight down and let them work as six. The pairing is the second reveal, and it reframes every note they wrote.

flights.title: WHY IS THIS ONE HOT?
flights.tag: 6 core + 4 extensions · ALL BLIND · ALL SIX BETWEEN 110 AND 113 PROOF · RANK THEM BY HEAT
flights.premise: Six bourbons inside three proof points — 110, 110.8, 111, 111.2, 111.6, 113. Effectively one strength. And yet they will not feel like one strength, because three different things are masking or amplifying the alcohol: sweetness hides it, rye sharpens it, and a blender’s hand smooths it. This is the exact inverse of Proof Is Not a Score. That flight varies strength and asks what you hear. This one freezes strength and asks why you still hear differences.
why: Gold = the finale. Rust = pour blind, no introduction. Grey = reference or bench pour. Colour, nose, palate and finish are prompts — say them after the room speaks, never before.

DO NOT SAY THE PROOFS ARE CLOSE until the ranking is written and collected. Told they are all the same strength, the room stops ranking and starts hunting for the trick. Told nothing, they rank honestly — and the reveal does the work.

B SHOULD READ HOTTEST AND F SHOULD READ GENTLEST, AND F IS THE HIGHER PROOF. Heigold is a high-rye mashbill — rye sharpens and dries, which the palate reads as heat. Dareringer is wheated AND PX-finished — the softest grain under the sweetest wine. F is 2.2 proof points ABOVE B and will almost certainly be called the calmest pour on the table.

A AND C ARE THE CONTROLS AND THEY ARE UNFINISHED. Russell’s and Remus have nothing between the room and the alcohol — no wine, no blending. Whatever heat they show at 110 and 111 is what this strength actually feels like. Everything else is measured against them.

D IS THE THIRD MECHANISM AND THE SUBTLEST. Barrell Cigar Blend is blended and finished — not sweetened the way E and F are, but smoothed by marrying many barrels. If the room places D between the controls and the wine-finished pours, they have separated blending from sweetening, which almost nobody does.
Do not tell them it is three pairs until after the reveal. Pour A through F straight down and let them work as six. The pairing is the second reveal, and it reframes every note they wrote.

flights.title: NO AGE STATED
flights.tag: 6 core + 4 extensions · ALL BLIND · ALL SIX AT EXACTLY 80 PROOF · THREE HOUSES, EACH POURED TWICE
flights.premise: The companion to Age Is Not a Flavour, and a different question. That flight asks whether you can hear the years. This one asks what happens when nobody tells you. Three distilleries, each bottling one whisky with a number on the label and one without — and all six at EXACTLY 80 proof, which is a tighter control than the bourbon flight can manage.
why: Gold = the finale. Rust = pour blind, no introduction. Grey = reference or bench pour. Colour, nose, palate and finish are prompts — say them after the room speaks, never before.

THE REAL VARIABLE IS NOT THE LABEL — IT IS WHO WAS IN CHARGE. An age statement constrains the blender to a minimum and says nothing about the mix. No age statement frees them to use whatever tastes right. So the unnumbered bottles are blended TO A TARGET and the numbered ones are constrained by what is in the warehouse. That predicts something: the NAS pours should be smoother and more resolved, the age-stated ones more angular.

IN ALL THREE PAIRS THE UNNUMBERED BOTTLE IS CHEAPER. $44.99 against $189.99, $44.99 against $74.99, $49.99 against $62.99. The ask is not only which is which — it is whether the number earned its money. Collect that answer in writing before any price is spoken.

SMOKE CLIMBS RATHER THAN PROOF, because proof cannot climb — all six are 80. Jameson is unpeated, Connemara lightly peated, Laphroaig heavily. Pour in that order and the pairs stay adjacent with nothing buried. This is the only flight here where the ladder is built from smoke.
COLLECT THE PRICE GUESSES IN WRITING BEFORE ANY REVEAL. This is the flight most likely to produce a genuinely uncomfortable moment, and the discomfort only lands if people have committed on paper.

flights.premise: New Riff bonds its ryes and its malt at exactly 100 proof — bottled-in-bond means one distillery, one distilling season, four years minimum, 100 proof. Pours A, B and C are that: three grains, one strength, every other variable frozen by an 1897 law. Then corn shows up, and it shows up at barrel proof, because New Riff does not bond its bourbon. That asymmetry is itself a finding.
why: Gold = the finale. Rust = pour blind, no introduction. Grey = reference or bench pour. Colour, nose, palate and finish are prompts — say them after the room speaks, never before.

A, B AND C ARE ALL EXACTLY 100 PROOF AND BOTTLED-IN-BOND. Not an arrangement I engineered — New Riff’s house policy, which means the Bottled-in-Bond Act is doing the experimental control. Malted rye, rye and barley at one strength from one distillery, one season, one warehouse. Every other grain flight here compares across distilleries and has to apologise for it.

A AGAINST B IS THE PAIR NOBODY EXPECTS. Both rye, same distillery, same proof — but A’s grain was MALTED before mashing and B’s was not. Malting softens the whole character, and most rooms guess the malted one is a bourbon. Ask which of the two is rye before you say either of them is.

C IS THE ONE THAT BREAKS PEOPLE. American single malt at 100 proof bottled-in-bond, from a Kentucky distillery, sitting between two ryes. Nobody expects barley in this company and almost nobody places it.

D, E AND F ARE WHERE CORN AND STRENGTH BOTH ARRIVE, AND THAT IS THE ASYMMETRY. New Riff bonds rye and malt at 100 but bottles bourbon at barrel proof — 110.3 and 114.1 here. So the flight cannot hold proof steady across all six, and the honest move is to say so and pour the bourbons last. F is B undiluted, which closes the loop.

PROOF CORRECTION: the 4 Year Single Barrel is 114.1, not the 100 I first assumed — single barrels are not bonded. The controlled trio is A, B and C. Six bottles, about $370, no allocation and no secondary market.

flights.title: RYE, TURNED UP
flights.tag: 6 core + 4 extensions · ALL BLIND · RYE SCRAMBLED, PROOF ASCENDS · THE COMPANION TO WHEAT
flights.premise: The sister flight to Wheat, Turned Up, and the other half of the same argument. Corn is the canvas; rye or wheat is the paint. Here rye climbs from none at all to all of it — 0, 10, 35, 51, 100 — while the proof climbs independently, so nobody can rank one by reading the other.
why: Gold = the finale. Rust = pour blind, no introduction. Grey = reference or bench pour. Colour, nose, palate and finish are prompts — say them after the room speaks, never before.

THE ASK: rank the six by RYE CONTENT, lowest to highest, and write a percentage on each. Nothing is spotted. Rye is far more perceptible than wheat — it is a flavour rather than an absence — so unlike the wheat flight, most rooms get roughly the right order. What they get wrong is the size of the gaps.

THE SCRAMBLE IS THE DESIGN. By rye the order runs 51, 10, 0, 100, 35, 100 — and by proof it runs 84.8 to 130.2 in a clean line. Anyone ranking by weight in the mouth will put A near the bottom and F at the top and be right for the wrong reason. C at 95 proof has NO rye whatsoever and will get guessed above B at 90, which has some.

D AND F ARE BOTH 100% RYE AND SHOULD NOT TASTE ALIKE. One is American, one Canadian, and Canada’s rye tradition is a different plant handled a different way. Twenty-four proof points apart, same grain bill, nothing else in common. Ask which is which before you say either is 100%.

THIS IS THE OTHER HALF OF WHEAT, TURNED UP. Run them a week apart and the pair answers the whole question: American whiskey chooses between exactly two flavouring grains, and this is what each one does when you turn it up.

RYE IS EASIER THAN WHEAT, AND THAT IS THE FINDING. Run it alongside Wheat, Turned Up and the room will notice they did far better here. Rye announces itself; wheat is defined by what it removes. Same experiment, opposite difficulty.

flights.tag: 9 core + 2 extensions · POUR 1 SPOTTED, POURS 2–6 BLIND — MATCH THE CASK
flights.premise: Old Elk runs the same base distillate across its finishing programme at nearly identical proof, so the only variable is wood. Pour 1 is named and shown — the unfinished control. why: Gold = the finale. Rust = pour blind, no introduction. Grey = reference or bench pour. Colour, nose, palate and finish are prompts — say them after the room speaks, never before.

Spotting the control is what makes the game playable. Name pour 1, show the bottle, and make the room describe it out loud before anything else is poured. Every glass after it is then a comparison against a fixed reference rather than a guess in open space — the difference between a puzzle and a shrug.

READ THE LIST ALOUD BEFORE POUR 2, and keep more options on it than there are glasses: Oloroso · Pedro Ximénez · tawny port · madeira · rum · Armagnac · COGNAC · Cabernet. Eight options, five pours. Nobody solves the last glass by elimination.

They sit at pours 3 and 6, deliberately apart, so nobody can A/B them. Before the cognac arrived, anyone who smelled grape had the Armagnac by elimination. Not any more.

Pour 7 is the coda and the contrast that carries the room. Same rum wood as one of the five they just matched, different country, different distillate. Ask which blind pour it rhymes with. This is the Connemara-against-Waterford move from Peat Is a Postcode, and it works for the same reason: the room already holds the category.

Pours 8 and 9 are pours 1 and 2 run again at four times the price and sixteen years older. The room hears the identical argument twice at two price points, and the repetition is what makes it stick. This is also the only flight where nothing steps down in proof.

flights.title: NEW CHARRED OAK IS THE LAW
flights.tag: 6 core + 4 extension pours · ALL BLIND · ONE VARIABLE: HOW MUCH OAK, AND HOW IT WAS TREATED
flights.premise: Bourbon is the only category on earth that legally requires NEW CHARRED OAK. Every producer starts from the same rule, so everything past it is a choice: a second barrel, a third, toast instead of char. Where the Tree Grew asks which species. This asks how much, and what the cooper did to it — and it can only be asked properly in bourbon, because bourbon is where the wood is mandatory.
why: Gold = the finale. Rust = pour blind, no introduction. Grey = reference or bench pour. Colour, nose, palate and finish are prompts — say them after the room speaks, never before.

POURS A, B AND C ARE THE SPINE, AND NOTHING ELSE ON YOUR SHELF CAN DO THIS. One distillery, one distillate, ONE PROOF — 90.4 for all three — through one barrel, then two, then three. Not proof, not age, not recipe. Just more wood, three times, at identical strength.

POURS D AND E ARE THE SAME IDEA IN OTHER HANDS. Two barrels and three from Jefferson’s and Angel’s Envy. Set D against B and E against C and the question becomes “whose more oak”. Most rooms find one house’s second barrel does more than another’s third.

POUR F IS THE TURN, AND IT CLOSES THE CORE. Char is burning the stave; toast is baking it. Char strips and filters, toast caramelises the sugars in the wood. They taste nothing alike and almost nobody has tasted them side by side deliberately. Pour F last, ask which pours it does NOT belong with, then bring the 20 Year Toasted off the bench while the question is still open.
PROOF IS DELIBERATELY FLAT — 90.4, 90.4, 90.4, 90.2, 92, 100. Five of six sit within two proof points, so nobody ranks by strength. The extensions break that on purpose, after the core lands.
Nothing to buy. Three Woodfords make the quantity argument at 90 proof in the core; three Barrells make the toast argument at cask strength on the bench. Ten bottles, all yours.

flights.title: WHERE THE TREE GREW
flights.tag: 6 core + 4 extensions · ALL BLIND · ONE VARIABLE: THE TREE. SPECIES AND PROVENANCE, NOT FINISHING.
flights.premise: One Barrel, Five Endings asks what a second cask ADDS. This asks what the wood IS. Six whiskies whose primary oak differs by species or by where the tree grew — Japanese mizunara, Portuguese virgin oak, standard American white oak, and the same Irish whiskey aged in oak from two different American states. Everyone talks about the barrel. Almost nobody tastes the tree.
why: Gold = the finale. Rust = pour blind, no introduction. Grey = reference or bench pour. Colour, nose, palate and finish are prompts — say them after the room speaks, never before.

E AND F ARE THE HARD PAIR AND THEY COME LAST FOR A REASON. Same whiskey, same distillery, same 101 proof, same species — Quercus alba — and the only difference is which American state the tree grew in. Missouri oak grows slower in a harsher climate, so the grain is tighter. Whether that survives into the glass is a genuinely open question, and a room that cannot separate them has learned something real about how far provenance carries.

THE CONTROL IS POUR C AND IT IS DELIBERATELY ORDINARY. New charred American white oak is the default the entire bourbon industry runs on, and most rooms have never tasted it as a reference point rather than as a drink. Establish it out loud before the exotic wood arrives, or the room has nothing to measure against.

MIZUNARA AND PORTUGUESE OAK CARRY THE FLIGHT. Japanese oak gives sandalwood and incense that no other wood gives; virgin Portuguese oak gives dry resin and green wood. Those two are unmistakable and they are what makes the evening work — pours A, B and D are the flight, and E and F are the question it leaves open.
PROOF ASCENDS — 86, 88, 90.4, 100, 101, 101 — and nothing here is peated, so neither strength nor smoke gives anything away. The only thing that changes is what the whiskey sat in.

THE ONE PURCHASE WORTH MAKING for this flight is the Chinquapin. It is a different species of American white oak, fully matured rather than finished, and it slots straight in beside E and F as a third American tree. $129.99, and I talked you out of it once when it had no home. It has one now.

flights.title: SHERRY IS NOT ONE THING
flights.tag: 6 core + 4 extensions · ALL BLIND · ALL SCOTCH, NO SMOKE · ONE VARIABLE: WHICH SHERRY
flights.premise: Almost everyone who says “sherried” means “sweet”. Sherry runs from bone dry to syrup, and the cask carries whichever one was in it. Six unpeated Scotch malts, five different sherry styles — Fino, Oloroso, Cream, Manzanilla, and all of them at once. Nothing here is peated, so the wine has nowhere to hide.
why: Gold = the finale. Rust = pour blind, no introduction. Grey = reference or bench pour. Colour, nose, palate and finish are prompts — say them after the room speaks, never before.

POUR A KILLS THE ASSUMPTION IN THIRTY SECONDS. Fino is the driest sherry made and Montilla is drier still — no sweetness whatsoever, saline and almond-skinned. Open here and the room’s definition of “sherried” breaks before anyone has formed a theory to defend. Everything afterwards is measured against a dry benchmark rather than a sweet one.

POUR E IS THE RAREST THING IN THE PROGRAMME. Manzanilla is Fino aged by the sea at Sanlúcar, and virtually nobody finishes whisky in it — a distillery festival bottling from 1998 stock is close to the only way to taste it. If the room has one memorable pour from any of these twelve flights, it will be this one.

D, E AND F ARE ONE DISTILLERY ACROSS THREE FESTIVAL YEARS. Bunnahabhain is unpeated in its core range, which is why it can be here — and its Fèis Île bottlings happen to cover cream, Manzanilla and a three-wood blend. That is a sherry programme laid out end to end, and none of it is available in a shop.

PROOF ASCENDS — 86, 86, 92, 102.4, 104.6, 106.6 — and the two at 86 are deliberately paired. A and B are the same strength and opposite ends of the sherry spectrum. If anyone reads the darker one as stronger, colour has beaten proof again.

DATA FLAG: the Fèis Île 2024 is logged at an MSRP of $1.00 — an error from the original export that is still unfixed. It is a distillery-exclusive bottling worth two to three hundred. Worth correcting before you value anything.

flights.title: FORTIFIED OR TABLE?
flights.tag: 6 core + 4 extensions · ALL BLIND · ALL SIX ARE BOURBON, ALL SIX SAW WINE · THREE OF EACH KIND
flights.premise: Everyone says “wine finish” as though it means one thing. It means two. Sherry, port and madeira are FORTIFIED — spirit added, sugar left in, oxidised on purpose. Cabernet and Bordeaux are TABLE wine — drier, tannic, no spirit added. Six bourbons here, every one finished in wine, three of each kind, and the proof climbs from 80 to 108 with the two kinds alternating the whole way.
why: Gold = the finale. Rust = pour blind, no introduction. Grey = reference or bench pour. Colour, nose, palate and finish are prompts — say them after the room speaks, never before.

ONE BINARY ASKED SIX TIMES: was the barrel holding something fortified or something dry? Fortified reads as raisin, molasses and sweetness — sugar that survived because the fermentation was stopped with spirit. Table wine reads as red fruit, tannin and grape skin. Those are different flavour families and the room does not need to name a grape to hear the difference.

THE TWO KINDS ALTERNATE ALL THE WAY UP. Table at 80, 100 and 108; fortified at 86.6, 94 and 101.3. Nobody can sort by strength and be right, and nobody can sort by sweetness alone either — A is the driest pour and the lowest proof, F is the driest at the top.

F IS THE CLEAREST STATEMENT IN THE COLLECTION. Bardstown Silver Oak uses barrels from a Napa Cabernet house that ages its own wine in AMERICAN oak rather than French — so the wood is the same species that held the bourbon, and only the wine changed. It is the purest table-wine pour you own and it closes the flight.

THIS IS THE FLIGHT ONE WHISKEY, FOUR VINEYARDS COULD NOT BE. That one asked which VINEYARD, which is past the point where anyone can answer. This asks which KIND of wine, which is a real perceptual line — and the failure of the finer version is what makes the coarser one worth running.

DO NOT SAY IT IS THREE AND THREE until the sheets are collected. And do not let anyone name a grape — the ask is the KIND of wine, not the varietal. A room hunting for Cabernet has already stopped listening for sweetness.

flights.title: THE GRAPE THAT WAS DISTILLED
flights.tag: 6 core + 4 extensions · ALL BLIND · ALL SIX FINISHED IN BRANDY · FIVE ARE GRAPE, ONE IS NOT
flights.premise: Fortified or Table? covers wine. This covers what happens when the wine is DISTILLED before it goes in the barrel. Cognac, Armagnac and Calvados are brandies — spirits, not wines — and a brandy cask leaves dried fruit, florals and a faint spirity edge rather than sugar or tannin. Six bourbons, six brandy casks, and the proof climbs from 100 to 118.
why: Gold = the finale. Rust = pour blind, no introduction. Grey = reference or bench pour. Colour, nose, palate and finish are prompts — say them after the room speaks, never before.

A AND B ARE THE PAIR AND THEY ARE 0.2 PROOF APART. Joseph Magnus Bourbon and Cigar Blend: same house, same base, same strength to a fifth of a point — and the only difference is that Cigar Blend adds ARMAGNAC on top of the cognac. One extra brandy, $110 extra, and nothing else moves. That is the tightest pair in the programme after Vantage.

E AND F DO IT AGAIN AT OLD ELK. One distillate, cognac against Armagnac — two French grape brandies that are genuinely different: cognac is double-distilled in pot stills and lighter; Armagnac is column-distilled once, earthier, with the rancio note that only comes with long oxidation. Same whiskey underneath both.

D IS THE ASK AND IT IS FINDABLE. Five of these saw grape brandy. Calvados is APPLE. Nobody needs to tell cognac from Armagnac — that is genuinely hard — but baked apple against dried grape is a line anyone can hear. Find the pour that never met a vine.

THIS IS THE THIRD CATEGORY OF WINE CASK AND THE ONE NOBODY NAMES. Sherry and port are fortified. Cabernet and Bordeaux are table. Cognac and Armagnac are neither — the wine was distilled first, so the sugar is gone and what is left is concentrated fruit and floral oak. Run this after Fortified or Table and the three categories close the whole subject.

DO NOT ASK ANYONE TO NAME THE BRANDY. Cognac against Armagnac is a specialist call and the flight does not need it. The ask is grape or apple, and which two pours share a house — both answerable, both in the glass.

flights.premise: One Barrel, Five Endings holds one distillate constant and changes the wood. This does the opposite: one cask type, six different whiskies underneath it. Irish pot still, New Zealand malt, Highland malt, wheated bourbon, Irish malt, and a blend of straight bourbons — every one of them finished in Pedro Ximénez. why: Gold = the finale. Rust = pour blind, no introduction. Grey = reference or bench pour. Colour, nose, palate and finish are prompts — say them after the room speaks, never before.
The wine goes first and it is not optional. Pour the straight PX neat and make the room name what they smell. It is the only fixed point; everything after is that same wine on six different surfaces.
Proof climbs the whole way — 92, 92, 101.6, 107.2, 112.4, 115.52 — so nothing needs watering and nothing steps down.
Pours 1 and 5 are both Irish and both PX — one single pot still, one single malt. Same country, same wine, different grain recipe. Call it out at pour 5 and have them look back at pour 1.

The finale is the biggest departure and the highest proof. Five malts and a pot still, then something that spent years in new charred American oak before it ever met a sherry butt. If PX tastes like one thing across all six, the wine is doing the work. If it does not, the spirit is. The room will not agree, and that disagreement is the point.

flights.title: DOES RYE TAKE A FINISH?
flights.tag: 6 core + 4 extensions · ALL BLIND · EVERY POUR IS RYE · ONE MATCHED PAIR AT EXACTLY 92 PROOF
flights.premise: Every other wood flight in this programme uses bourbon or malt as the base. This one uses rye, and it tests a claim people repeat without checking: that rye RESISTS finishing. Bourbon’s corn sweetness absorbs a wine cask; rye’s pepper and herb are supposed to fight it. Six ryes, one of them unfinished, and the ask is how much rye survived.
why: Gold = the finale. Rust = pour blind, no introduction. Grey = reference or bench pour. Colour, nose, palate and finish are prompts — say them after the room speaks, never before.

A AND B ARE THE FLIGHT AND NOTHING ELSE NEEDS TO WORK. Same distillery, same rye, same 92 proof — one given a sherry cask and one not. Every other variable is gone. Pour them consecutively and ask a single question: is the pepper still there? If B keeps its spine, the folklore holds. If the sherry buried it, rye is as absorbent as anything else.

THE LADDER CLIMBS IN AGGRESSION, NOT JUST PROOF. Sherry at 92 and 94, port and French oak at 98.6, rum at 100, and then three casks at once at 120.2. Each pour asks more of the rye than the one before it, so where the room stops finding pepper is the answer.

E IS THE HARDEST TEST AND THE CHEAPEST BOTTLE HERE. Rum is sugar cane — molasses and banana against a grain built on pepper and dill. They have nothing in common, which is exactly why Angel’s Envy tried it. If any pour loses its rye entirely, this is the one.

F THROWS EVERYTHING AT IT. Martinique rhum, Madeira and apricot brandy, on a rye, at 120.2 proof. It should be a mess and it is not — which is the strongest evidence for the folklore on the page. Pour it last and ask whether the rye is still leading.

VERIFY THE HEAVEN’S DOOR PAIR BEFORE THE NIGHT. The flight assumes Refuge is the straight rye given a sherry cask — read both labels and confirm they share a base. If they do not, A and B stop being a matched pair and the flight loses its only clean control.

flights.title: CAN YOU FIND THE AMERICANS?
flights.tag: 6 core + 4 extensions · ALL BLIND · THREE ARE AMERICAN. THREE ARE NOT.
flights.premise: American single malt got its federal standard in 2025. The question this flight asks is whether it tastes American — or whether it tastes like whatever its maker was copying. Six unpeated single malts between 88 and 93 proof, three from the United States and three from Scotland and Ireland. No proof tells, no peat to hide behind. Sort them.
why: Gold = the finale. Rust = pour blind, no introduction. Grey = reference or bench pour. Colour, nose, palate and finish are prompts — say them after the room speaks, never before.

THE ASK IS PREFERENCE, NOT POWER. Which pour is stronger is obvious in a second and nobody gets credit for it. Two columns: guess the proof, then rate whether you would rather drink it. The second column is the flight — the same structure that works in Age Is Not a Flavour.
Proof runs 88 to 93 across all six, which removes the crutch everyone reaches for. Nobody can sort these by strength, and none of them is peated, so the usual shortcuts are gone.

The finding is the point, and it may not be flattering. American single malt has no house style yet — the category is too young. Some chases Scotch, some chases bourbon, some goes its own way. If the room cannot reliably pick the Americans, that IS the answer to the question on the card.

Watch pour D. Bladnoch is Lowland — light, gentle, no smoke, no sherry — and it is the pour most rooms call American. Craigellachie at C is the opposite trap: worm tubs give it a sulphury, meaty edge nobody expects from Speyside, and people reach for "craft distillery" to explain it.
Reveal by pour letter, not by country — let them watch their own sheet get marked up.

flights.title: IRELAND MAKES FOUR THINGS
flights.tag: 6 core + 4 extensions · ALL BLIND · ONE COUNTRY, FOUR LEGAL CATEGORIES · TWO MATCHED PAIRS
flights.premise: Ireland is the only whiskey country with four legally distinct categories, and one of them exists nowhere else on earth. Single malt is all malted barley. SINGLE POT STILL is malted AND unmalted barley in one mash — an Irish invention that began as a tax dodge in 1785. Single grain is column-distilled from corn and wheat. A blend is any of those married together. Six pours, four definitions, and two of the pairs come from the same distillery at the same proof.
why: Gold = the finale. Rust = pour blind, no introduction. Grey = reference or bench pour. Colour, nose, palate and finish are prompts — say them after the room speaks, never before.

B AND C ARE ONE DISTILLERY AT ONE PROOF IN TWO CATEGORIES. Powers Gold Label and Powers Three Swallow, both 86.4, both from Midleton — one a blend, one a single pot still. The legal category is the ONLY variable and it is frozen on everything else. That is the flight, and almost no collection can pour it.

D AND E DO IT AGAIN AT TEELING. Single grain and single pot still, both 92, both Dublin. Grain whiskey is the category nobody has knowingly tasted — it is what fills out most blends and it is almost never bottled alone. Poured beside its own distillery’s pot still, the difference between column and pot distillation stops being a diagram.

RUN IT BEFORE Can You Find the Americans. That flight leans on Irish malts as the non-American pours, and a room that has already learned what pot still tastes like will find it considerably harder — which is the right direction for difficulty to move.

PROOF ASCENDS — 80, 86.4, 86.4, 92, 92, 108.4 — with the two matched pairs sitting at identical numbers. F is the only cask-strength pour and the only one over $150; it is also a blend, which is the category people rank lowest before they taste it.
The line: single pot still is the only category invented to avoid a tax and kept because it tasted better. · SNACKS: brown bread, salted butter, mild cheddar, plain crackers.

flights.title: IS TENNESSEE JUST FILTERED BOURBON?
flights.tag: 6 core + 4 extensions · ALL BLIND · THE LINCOLN COUNTY PROCESS, AND WHETHER YOU CAN TASTE IT
flights.premise: Tennessee whiskey is bourbon by every measure except one: before barrelling, the new spirit is filtered through several feet of sugar-maple charcoal. That is the Lincoln County Process, and it is a legal requirement. The whole category rests on whether it does anything you can taste — and one bottle here settles the argument by printing BOURBON on a Tennessee label.
why: Gold = the finale. Rust = pour blind, no introduction. Grey = reference or bench pour. Colour, nose, palate and finish are prompts — say them after the room speaks, never before.

POUR B IS THE WHOLE ARGUMENT AND IT IS PRINTED ON THE BOTTLE. Peg Leg Porker calls itself Tennessee Straight BOURBON — legally accurate, and a refusal to hide behind the category. Pour it blind and ask which pours are Tennessee. If B gets called Kentucky, the label was right.

A AND C USE DIFFERENT PROCESSES AND ALMOST NOBODY KNOWS IT. Jack Daniel’s filters at room temperature and Gentleman Jack does it TWICE, before and after ageing. Dickel chills the spirit first. Same legal requirement, two executions, and that difference is more audible than the difference from bourbon.

THE CONTROL IS ON THE BENCH AND YOU MUST POUR IT. Buffalo Trace at 90 against Peg Leg Porker at 90: identical strength, one charcoal-filtered and one not. That pair answers the card better than the other five pours combined.

POUR F HAS THE BEST STORY ON THE PAGE. Nathan “Nearest” Green was the enslaved man who taught Jack Daniel to distil, and the charcoal process this entire flight is built on is his. Tell it at the reveal, not before — it will end the blind tasting the moment it is said.

The line: the difference is several feet of sugar-maple charcoal. Whether that is a category or a marketing department is what the room is here to decide. · SNACKS: salted pecans, mild cheddar, pretzels.

flights.title: THREE MILES APART
flights.tag: 6 core + 4 extensions · ALL BLIND · ONE ISLAND, SIX DISTILLERIES · THE INVERSE OF PEAT IS A POSTCODE
flights.premise: Islay is twenty-five miles long. Peat Is a Postcode argued that place makes the smoke; this flight tests that claim where it should be easiest to prove and turns out to be hardest. Pours A, B and C come from three distilleries on the same stretch of the same southern shore, within about three miles of each other, mostly using barley malted at the same commercial maltings. If place makes the whisky, those three should be near-identical. They are not remotely.
why: Gold = the finale. Rust = pour blind, no introduction. Grey = reference or bench pour. Colour, nose, palate and finish are prompts — say them after the room speaks, never before.

A, B AND C ARE NEIGHBOURS. Laphroaig, Lagavulin and Ardbeg sit in that order along a few miles of the Kildalton coast — you can walk between them in an afternoon — and most of their malt comes from the same place. Pour them consecutively and ask the room how far apart they are. Nobody guesses three miles.

SO WHAT IS DOING THE WORK? Still shape, cut points, fermentation time, and wood policy. Laphroaig ferments and cuts for medicine; Lagavulin runs slower and sweeter; Ardbeg cuts later and keeps the citric, sooty end. All three are choices made indoors. The peat is nearly common ground.

D IS UNDISCLOSED AND THAT IS THE POINT. Smokehead says only “an Islay distillery”. Have the room name which one, in writing, before the reveal — and then tell them the truth is that nobody outside Ian Macleod knows for certain. Watching a room commit confidently to an unanswerable question is worth doing once.

E AND F ARE THE FAR ENDS OF THE ISLAND and they are NOT the outliers. West Islay and north Islay, twenty-odd miles from the Kildalton three — and the gap between B and C is bigger than the gap between C and F. That is the finding, and it undoes the flight it is named against.
RUN THIS AFTER PEAT IS A POSTCODE, NOT BEFORE. That flight establishes that place changes smoke. This one narrows the frame until the claim breaks. In the wrong order it is just six Islay whiskies.

flights.title: ONE STILL, TWO FAMILIES

flights.premise: Midleton makes Redbreast and the Spot range from the same single pot still spirit — the same mash of malted and unmalted barley, through the same stills, in the same County Cork distillery. They are sold as distinct traditions with separate histories. Six bottles here, three from each family, and every one at EXACTLY 92 proof. why: Gold = the finale. Rust = pour blind, no introduction. Grey = reference or bench pour. Colour, nose, palate and finish are prompts — say them after the room speaks, never before.

C AGAINST D IS THE FLIGHT. Redbreast 15 and Red Spot 15: same still, same spirit, same FIFTEEN YEARS, same 92 proof. The only difference is that one finished in Oloroso and the other in Marsala. Everything a distillery can control is frozen except the wood — and the two brands cost $139.99 and $204.99.

THE ASK IS FAMILY, NOT BRAND. Mark each pour REDBREAST or SPOT. Nobody needs to name a bottling, and neither age nor proof varies enough to help. If the families are genuinely distinct traditions, the split should be findable. If they are one whiskey in two liveries, nobody gets above chance.

THIS IS THE QUESTION ODDLY SIMILAR COULD NOT ASK. That flight was cut because its answer was a fact about sourcing you had to be told. This one has the same shape — one distillery behind several labels — and the answer is entirely in the glass, because the cask programmes really do differ and everything else is held still.

THE SPOTS LEAN ON WINE AND REDBREAST LEANS ON SHERRY. Yellow Spot uses Malaga, Red Spot uses Marsala, Gold Spot uses four woods. Redbreast is bourbon and Oloroso, over and over. flights.title: CAN YOU TELL WHO’S BIG?
flights.tag: 6 core + 4 extensions · ALL BLIND · THREE MAJORS, THREE CRAFT · NOTHING FINISHED, NOTHING FLAVOURED
flights.premise: Three whiskeys from companies that fill millions of barrels, three from small producers. Every pour is straight — no wine casks, no finishes, no flavouring. That is deliberate: craft distillers finish more often than majors do, so a finished pour would let the room identify the craft ones by technique rather than by anything about the whiskey itself.
why: Gold = the finale. Rust = pour blind, no introduction. Grey = reference or bench pour. Colour, nose, palate and finish are prompts — say them after the room speaks, never before.

THE ASK: mark each pour BIG or CRAFT, then rank all six for preference. Two columns, and the second one is where the flight lives. Almost everyone believes small means better and almost nobody has tested it blind against price.

BOTH ENDS ARE DELIBERATELY CROSSED. Your craft bottles skew high-proof and your majors skew low, so a lazy room could sort by strength and be right by accident. A is craft at 82 — the LOWEST proof here — and E is a major at 116.8. Anyone sorting by weight gets both ends backwards.

E AGAINST F IS THE HONEST FIGHT. Wild Turkey Rare Breed at 116.8 and $59.99, against Davidson Reserve at 118 and $41.99. Nearly identical proof, and the CRAFT one is cheaper. Rare Breed is among the most respected bourbons made at any price and it comes from a company that fills more barrels in a week than Pennington fills in a year. Whichever way this pair goes, somebody’s assumption breaks.

D IS A CRAFT BRAND THAT DOES NOT DISTIL, AND F IS A CRAFT DISTILLERY. Belle Meade is Nelson’s Greenbrier blending sourced barrels; Davidson Reserve is Pennington making their own. Both are small companies, and only one of them made the whiskey. Say that at the reveal — a small company and a small distillery are not the same thing, and the label rarely tells you which you are holding.

flights.title: DOES HOUSE STYLE SURVIVE PEAT?
flights.tag: 6 core + 4 extensions · ALL BLIND · THREE DISTILLERIES, EACH POURED TWICE — ONCE SMOKED, ONCE NOT
flights.premise: Three distilleries that make both a peated and an unpeated whisky from the same spirit, the same water and the same stills. Two of the pairs are bottled at IDENTICAL proof — 92.6 and 100 — so within a pair the only thing that changed is whether the barley met smoke. Finding the peated pours is trivial. Finding which two belong together is not, and that is the entire flight.
why: Gold = the finale. Rust = pour blind, no introduction. Grey = reference or bench pour. Colour, nose, palate and finish are prompts — say them after the room speaks, never before.

THE ASK IS NOT WHICH ARE PEATED. Everyone gets that in one sniff and nobody earns anything for it. The ask is WHICH TWO POURS SHARE A DISTILLERY — three pairs, six glasses, and the room has to hear past the smoke to whatever is underneath it.

TWO PAIRS ARE AT IDENTICAL PROOF. Bunnahabhain at 92.6 and 92.6, Bruichladdich at 100 and 100. Not close — the same number. Within those pairs, peat is the only variable that exists. The Benriach pair moves 86 to 92, which is the one place strength could help, so treat pair one as the easier warm-up.

WHAT THE ANSWER MEANS EITHER WAY. If the room finds all three pairs, house character survives smoke and peat is a coat of paint. If it finds none, peat overwrites the distillery entirely and Peat Is a Postcode was measuring the wrong thing. Most rooms find one or two — and WHICH ones they find is the real result.

THIS IS THE FLIGHT PEAT IS A POSTCODE COULD NOT ASK. That night proved smoke differs by place. This asks whether the place still shows through the smoke — and it can only be asked with distilleries that bottle both, which is three of yours and almost nobody else’s.

POUR AS PAIRS OR STRAIGHT DOWN — your choice, and it changes the difficulty. Poured A to F in order, the pairs sit adjacent and the flight is fair. Shuffled, it becomes genuinely hard. Do not tell the room there are three pairs until the sheets are collected.

flights.title: DOES A SECOND CASK HELP?

flights.premise: Diageo runs a Distillers Edition programme: take the standard bottling, give it a second maturation in a named wine cask, bottle it at the same strength. You own three complete pairs — inland Highland, coastal Highland and Islay — and every one of the six is at EXACTLY 86 proof. Not five of six, not within a point. Six bottles, one number, and the only variable inside a pair is whether it got a second cask.
why: Gold = the finale. Rust = pour blind, no introduction. Grey = reference or bench pour. Colour, nose, palate and finish are prompts — say them after the room speaks, never before.

THE ASK IS WHICH TWO POURS SHARE A DISTILLERY, then which half of each pair you would rather drink. The first question is hard and findable. The second is the one worth arguing about — a second cask is a decision someone made on purpose, and the room gets to judge it.

THE PROGRAMME IS THE CONSTANT AND THE DISTILLERY IS THE VARIABLE, which is the reverse of every other cask flight here. One Barrel, Five Endings changes the cask on one distillate. This holds one company’s technique steady and changes what it is applied to — and nothing else in the programme runs that direction.

D AND F ARE OPPOSITE ENDS OF THE SAME FAMILY. Oban gets Montilla Fino, the driest sherry made. Lagavulin gets PX, the sweetest. Same programme, same company, and the two finishes could not be further apart — which tells you Diageo is not applying a formula, it is answering each spirit separately.

If the DE improves the Dalwhinnie but muddies the Lagavulin, that is a finding about which spirits need help — a delicate Highland has room for more; a heavily peated Islay may already be full. Do not push the room toward “better”. Two of these three pairs may go the other way.

POUR E AND F LAST, ALWAYS — they are the only peated pair and they would end any comparison that followed them. Otherwise pour straight down A to F: the pairs sit adjacent and the flight is fair. Shuffle only if the room has done this before.

ALL SIX ARE 90 PROOF AND THAT IS THE WHOLE DESIGN. Not five of six, not within a point — six bottles at the same number from one company. flights.title: DOES A FINISHING HOUSE HAVE A STYLE?
flights.tag: 6 core + 4 extensions · POUR A SPOTTED, THE REST BLIND · FOUR OF SIX ARE THE SAME FINISH AT FOUR STRENGTHS
flights.premise: Angel’s Envy finishes everything it makes. Port on the flagship, madeira on one, sherry on the single barrels — a second cask is the house’s entire identity. Triple Oak is the exception: three oak types and no wine anywhere. Pour it FIRST and spotted, so the room meets the house undressed, and every glass after it is measured against something rather than guessed at.
why: Gold = the finale. Rust = pour blind, no introduction. Grey = reference or bench pour. Colour, nose, palate and finish are prompts — say them after the room speaks, never before.

A IS SPOTTED AND POURED FIRST FOR A REASON. Every other flight here hides the control. This one hands it over, because the question is not WHICH pour has no wine — it is HOW MUCH OF A IS STILL IN EACH OF THE OTHERS. A room measuring against something answers a better question than a room hunting for something.

FOUR OF THE SIX ARE THE SAME PORT FINISH AT FOUR STRENGTHS. B at 86.6, D at 111.6, E at 118.2, F at 119.8 — one wine, thirty-three proof points. That is a proof ladder inside a single cask decision, and it means the room is not sorting six finishes. It is sorting one wine at four volumes, with two departures.

C IS THE ONLY POUR THAT IS NOT PORT AND THAT IS THE BLIND QUESTION. Madeira is drier and nuttier than port — dried apricot and walnut against raisin and maple. Find it. In a flight where the control is given away, this is the only thing genuinely hidden.

THE HONEST RESULT MAY BE THAT THERE IS NO HOUSE STYLE. If A tastes like a different distillery from B through F, then Angel’s Envy is a finishing programme rather than a distillery, and the port is the product. That is a legitimate answer and the room should be allowed to reach it.
POUR A FIRST, NAMED, AND LEAVE IT IN FRONT OF EVERYONE FOR THE WHOLE FLIGHT. It is a reference, not a round. People should be going back to it after every glass.

flights.title: FOUR WAYS TO WOOD A LAPHROAIG
flights.tag: 6 core + 4 extensions · ALL BLIND · FOUR POURS AT EXACTLY 96 PROOF · ONE SPIRIT, FOUR WOOD STRATEGIES
flights.premise: One distillery, one peat level, one spirit — and four bottlings at EXACTLY 96 proof that each use wood a different way. Smaller casks. Sherry. PX. Many cask types married together. The standard 10 opens at 80 and the cask strength closes at 117.2, so the middle four are held at one number and the only thing that moves between them is the cooperage decision.
why: Gold = the finale. Rust = pour blind, no introduction. Grey = reference or bench pour. Colour, nose, palate and finish are prompts — say them after the room speaks, never before.

B, C, D AND E ARE ALL EXACTLY 96 PROOF. Four bottlings, one number, one spirit, one peat level — and four completely different answers to what wood should do. Cask SIZE, sherry, PX, and a marriage of many. Strength cannot help the room and neither can smoke, because all four carry the same amount.

B IS THE ONE PEOPLE NEVER THINK ABOUT. Quarter Cask changes the SIZE of the barrel, not its contents — a smaller cask means more wood touching every drop and faster extraction. It is the only pour here where the variable is geometry rather than a previous occupant, and it is the flight’s quiet lesson.

A AND F BRACKET EVERYTHING AND SHARE A RECIPE. Both are the standard 10 in ex-bourbon; one is cut to 80 and one is not cut at all. Pour A first and F last, and the room measures the four wood decisions against a spirit they have already met twice at two strengths.

THE ASK: which pour saw the SMALLEST cask, and which saw the SWEETEST wine? Two questions, both answerable, and neither is “which is peated” — they all are, identically. This is the only flight in the programme where peat is a constant rather than a variable.

THE MIDDLE FOUR ARE THE FLIGHT AND THEY ARE INTERCHANGEABLE IN ORDER. Pour B to E in any sequence — there is no proof ladder to protect because there is no proof difference. Shuffle them if the room has done this before.

flights.title: WHAT ARDBEG CHANGED
flights.tag: 6 core + 4 extensions · ALL BLIND · ONE DISTILLERY — AND EACH RELEASE CHANGES EXACTLY ONE THING
flights.premise: Most distillery ranges are a ladder of age and proof. Ardbeg’s is not. Each release takes the standard whisky and alters ONE step in how it is made — the still, the malt, the years, the wood — and leaves everything else alone. Pour A is the control. The other five each broke one rule, and the ask is which rule each of them broke.
why: Gold = the finale. Rust = pour blind, no introduction. Grey = reference or bench pour. Colour, nose, palate and finish are prompts — say them after the room speaks, never before.

B IS THE POUR NOTHING ELSE ON YOUR SHELF CAN DO. Ardbeg’s spirit still carries a purifier — a copper tube that sends heavier vapour back for redistillation — and it is why Ardbeg tastes citric and bright while carrying more peat than Laphroaig. Heavy Vapours took it out. Same barley, same peat, same 92 proof, different plumbing. Still geometry as a tastable variable appears nowhere else in this programme.

A AND B ARE AT IDENTICAL PROOF AND THAT IS THE WHOLE CONTROL. 92 and 92, both ex-bourbon, both the house peating level. Pour them consecutively. If the room cannot separate them, a piece of copper does not matter as much as Ardbeg’s marketing says. If it can, the still is doing more than the wood.

D IS SMOKE THAT IS NOT PEAT. Ardcore uses roasted black malt — the grain is burnt, not the fuel. It reads as smoky and it is a different smoky: espresso and cocoa rather than tar and iodine. Anyone who has decided Ardbeg means peat will misplace it, and separating burnt grain from burnt peat is the hardest call here.

THE ASK: each pour changed ONE thing from A. Name it — still, age, malt or wood. Four options, five pours, so at least two share an answer. Do not tell the room that E and F are both wood; letting them argue about whether the difference between those two is a cask or a proof is the most useful conversation the flight produces.

POUR IN ORDER, NOT SHUFFLED. The proof ladder is 92, 92, 94.8, 100.2, 108.4, 114.2 and it climbs for a reason — D onwards would flatten anything poured after them. The two 92s go first together, which is where the flight lives.

flights.title: WHO’S YOUR DADDY?
flights.tag: 6 core + 4 extensions · ALL BLIND · TWO POURS NOT YET ON THE SHELF · PROOF ASCENDS 90 → 114
flights.premise: The only flight here that tests folklore rather than a variable. “Poor man’s Pappy” is Weller 12 married with Weller Antique 107, and the claim is that it approximates Van Winkle at a fraction of the price. A AGAINST B IS THE CLEANEST COMPARISON IN YOUR COLLECTION. Weller 12 and Lot B: same mashbill, same distillery, same twelve years, half a proof point apart. Every variable gone except which barrels Julian Van Winkle selected and which went into Weller.

D AGAINST E IS THE SAME TEST WITH FIVE YEARS ADDED. Both 107, both the same recipe. Now the question is whether age or selection is doing the work — and the room can answer it by comparing how far apart A/B are against how far apart D/E are.

flights.title: PEAT IS A POSTCODE
flights.tag: 6 core + 4 extensions = 10 bottles · ALL SIX POURED BLIND, A–F · Unpeated Campbeltown in, peated Campbeltown out
flights.premise: Smoke is not one thing. Where the peat was cut, what grew in it, and how the barley was kilned change the smoke more than the ppm number does. This flight opens and closes in the same small town on the Kintyre peninsula, once without peat and once with it — and the highest-ppm pour of the night is neither Scottish nor, legally, whisky.
why: Gold = the finale. Rust = pour blind, no introduction. Grey = reference or bench pour. Colour, nose, palate and finish are prompts — say them after the room speaks, never before.
Glen Scotia goes FIRST and unpeated. Its character is subtle — sea air, tropical fruit, oily texture — and it vanishes behind anything smoky. Establish the baseline while the palate is clean.

Pour 2 is the flight’s whole argument. At 54 ppm it carries MORE peat than the cask-strength Laphroaig at pour 5 — Canadian barley smoked on Vancouver Island — and tastes nothing like Islay. Rank 2 against 5 for ppm out loud before any reveal. Young and hot at twenty months — say that much even while blind, or it reads as a flaw.

The 2021 Longrow specifically. Every release is 46% and NCF, but the cask recipe is rewritten annually — 2022 is 100% sherry, 2024 is 90% sherry with port. Your Glen Scotia is 100% first-fill bourbon, so the more sherry in the Longrow the more the wood confounds the variable you are isolating. 2021 is the most bourbon-forward release documented.

Connemara at 80 sits third — Irish peat, no medicinal edge, the gentlest thing here before Islay arrives. Pour 4 names the single Irish field its barley grew in — the thesis of this flight printed on a label the room will not see — and it is ex-bourbon only, so nothing but place is doing the work. The Raasay Dùn Cana held a slot here until its label turned out to say Oloroso and PX quarter casks — the same confound the Longrow choice avoids — so it moved to One Wine, Six Whiskies.

Proof runs 92, 92, 80, 100, 117.2, 92. The dip at the end is the reward, not an anticlimax — after cask-strength Laphroaig a mature 92-proof Campbeltown reads as relief. Pours 2 and 6 are both 92 proof and about nineteen years apart.
